HRA capital expenditure is £22.39m in 2026/27 and then £12.25m and £13.25m. The paper does not give the reasons for the fall after 2026/27.
findings.matters: A fall in planned capital spend of this size from one year to the next changes future borrowing need, which lenders and peer councils would need to understand when comparing programmes.

findings.headline: General fund financing costs forecast to rise from 9.37% of net revenue stream in 2025/26 to 15.05% in 2027/28.

findings.detail: The paper says cash balances were high in the first half because business rates and council tax are received before they are paid out. It expects balances to fall as those payments go out, as capital spending continues, and as the February 2027 borrowing repayment is made.
findings.matters: Balances that build up in the first half and then run down are a seasonal pattern that finance directors manage through liquidity and cash-flow planning, and that lenders and peers look at when judging short-term cash position.

findings.headline: Knights Reach temporary accommodation lease to add a £38,864,542 asset and liability in 2026/27

findings.detail: HRA Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to decline over the period from £23.34m (31.03.26 actual) to £14.64m (31.03.29 estimate). HRA financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream are also declining from 16.38% in 2025/26 to 12.47% in 2028/29. This improving HRA position contrasts materially with the rising General Fund financing burden.
findings.matters: Demonstrates divergent trends across the council; improving HRA position may provide some financial flexibility to offset General Fund pressures, relevant to peer councils and to understanding overall council financial trajectory.
findings.figures: HRA CFR £23.34m (31.03.26) declining to £14.64m (31.03.29); HRA financing costs proportion 16.38% (2025/26) declining to 12.47% (2028/29)

findings.headline: IFRS16 lease capitalization of £41.14m represents 41% of planned 2026/27 capital expenditure
findings.detail: The Council adopted IFRS16 in 2024/25, requiring leases to be recognized on the balance sheet as right-of-use assets. In 2026/27, £41.14m of the reported capital expenditure relates to this accounting treatment, representing capitalization of existing lease arrangements rather than new capital investment. This is material context for interpreting the apparent capital expenditure increase.
findings.matters: Clarifies that over 40% of the reported capital increase is accounting-driven rather than new investment; important for lenders assessing actual capital program intensity and for peer councils planning similar accounting treatments.
findings.figures: £41.14m right-of-use assets in 2026/27 out of £99.82m total capital expenditure
findings.quote: In 2024/25 the Council adopted IFRS16 an accounting standard which requires the Council to recognise leases on the balance sheet as right-of-use assets.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs rising to 14.79% of net revenue stream in 2027/28, up from 10.30% in 2025/26
findings.detail: General Fund financing costs are forecast to rise from 10.30% of net revenue stream in 2025/26 actual to 13.02% in 2026/27 budget, peaking at 14.79% in 2027/28 before declining to 13.53% in 2028/29. This represents an increasing proportion of the revenue budget consumed by debt service, indicating growing affordability pressure.
findings.matters: Financing costs as a proportion of revenue is the statutory affordability indicator for council sustainability; rising to 14.79% indicates tightening financial flexibility and reduced capacity for discretionary spending or reserves building.
findings.figures: General Fund proportion of net revenue stream: 10.30% (2025/26 actual), 13.02% (2026/27 budget), 14.79% (2027/28 budget), 13.53% (2028/29 budget)
findings.quote: Proportion of net revenue stream 9.37% 10.30% 13.02% 14.79% 13.53%

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to increase from £28.00m to £67.46m in one year
findings.detail: The Council's underlying need to borrow for capital purposes will more than double from £28.00m (31.03.26) to £67.46m (31.03.27). This is driven by a sharp increase in General Fund CFR from £4.66m to £47.02m, offsetting a decline in HRA CFR from £23.34m to £20.44m. The increase reflects the capital expenditure planned for financing through borrowing net of revenue provision.
findings.matters: Capital Financing Requirement measures underlying borrowing need; doubling in one year indicates a significant shift in the council's capital financing position that affects credit assessment and peer council policy planning.
findings.figures: Total CFR £28.00m to £67.46m; General Fund CFR £4.66m to £47.02m; HRA CFR £23.34m to £20.44m

findings.headline: Capital expenditure planned to increase from £31.39m to £99.82m in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Council plans a major increase in capital spending in 2026/27, more than threefold the 2025/26 actual outturn. A significant portion (£41.14m) relates to IFRS16 lease recognition, which is an accounting treatment rather than new capital spending. A further potential increase of £1.091m is pending approval of adjusted balances in Appendix C.
findings.matters: Large capital programs require significant financing and indicate future borrowing needs; material change in capital intensity affects debt position and borrowing costs relevant to lenders and peer councils.
findings.figures: Total expenditure £31.39m (2025/26 actual), £99.82m (2026/27 estimate); right-of-use assets £41.14m; potential further increase £1.091m
findings.quote: Total Expenditure 31.39 99.82 37.97 28.89

findings.headline: Liability benchmark remains negative through forecast period, indicating no borrowing requirement and strong reserve position.
findings.detail: The council's liability benchmark—comparing actual borrowing against the minimum needed to fund capital plans—is negative throughout: -£153.14m (2026), -£126.32m (2027), -£111.78m (2028), and -£102.64m (2029). A negative benchmark indicates accumulated reserves and capital receipts exceed capital financing needs. Actual debt is declining from £23.34m to £14.64m despite the CFR increase, confirming the council funds the lease commitment from reserves rather than external borrowing.
findings.matters: A negative liability benchmark indicates strong financial resilience and reduced refinancing risk. It demonstrates the council can absorb the major lease commitment and other capital investment without additional borrowing, sustaining financial flexibility.
findings.quote: Both the medium-term forecast in table 2 above and the longer-term forecast shows the liability benchmark is negative, representing that the Council has no need to borrow for the foreseeable future.

findings.headline: General fund financing costs as proportion of revenue stream rise to 14.54% in 2027/28, peak in forecast period.
findings.detail: Annual financing costs (interest and Minimum Revenue Provision on debt and lease obligations) are forecast to consume an increasing share of the revenue budget in the general fund. The proportion rises from 10.30% in 2025/26 to 12.80% in 2026/27, peaks at 14.54% in 2027/28, then declines to 13.54% in 2028/29. In cash terms, general fund financing costs increase from £2.82m to £3.61m and £3.60m respectively. This represents a material increase in the revenue budget burden of long-term liabilities.
findings.matters: Financing costs consume revenue budget that would otherwise be available for services. An increase to 14.54% represents significant revenue pressure in the medium term and indicates reduced financial flexibility for the council.
findings.quote: Although capital expenditure is not charged directly to the revenue budget, interest payable on loans and repayments are charged to revenue. The net annual charge is known as financing costs; this is compared to the net revenue stream i.e. the amount funded from Council Tax, business rates and general government grants.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement more than doubles from £28m to £67.87m due to lease recognition.
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement, measuring the council's underlying need to borrow, increases from £28.00m (31.3.2026 actual) to £67.87m forecast for 31.3.2027 before stabilizing around £69m in subsequent years. This increase reflects the lease liability recognition. Despite the CFR doubling, actual debt is declining from £23.34m to £14.64m, indicating the council is not externally borrowing against this liability.
findings.matters: The CFR is a key prudential indicator of future borrowing requirement and long-term financial commitment. A doubling signals material change in the council's capital structure that affects treasury management strategy and refinancing risk.
findings.quote: The CFR increases in 26/27 due to the recognition of the 55-year lease for 139 properties. As the Council makes MRP each year this figure will reduce.

findings.headline: Council committing to 55-year lease for 139 temporary accommodation properties with capital value of £40.14m.
findings.detail: The council is entering into a long-term lease arrangement for temporary accommodation properties. The accounting rules require recognition of the present value of future lease payments as capital expenditure, estimated at £40.14m at current PWLB rates, with the lease scheduled to commence in autumn 2026/27. This single item more than doubles the capital programme from £37.58m to £101.57m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: This represents a major 55-year financial commitment that fundamentally changes the council's balance sheet and debt profile, with implications for borrowing capacity and revenue sustainability across five decades.
findings.figures: £40.14m capital value at current PWLB rates; 55-year lease term; 139 properties; drives 2026/27 capital programme from £37.58m to £101.57m
findings.quote: The Council is due to entered into a 55-year lease arrangement for 139 properties for temporary accommodation. The Council has to recognise the discounted value of the future lease payments under this arrangement as capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Chestnut Grove playground works exceeded budget by £37,000 due to delays and extra work
findings.detail: Playground improvements project that rolled forward from 2025/26 finished in early 2026 but incurred additional costs beyond the rolled-forward budget allowance.
findings.matters: Scheme-level cost overrun; demonstrates budget planning and/or contingency issues
findings.figures: £37,000 overspend
findings.quote: due to delays and extra work required the final costs have exceeded the budget by £37,000.

findings.headline: General Fund capital budget reduced by £0.197m due to 2025/26 overspend, constraining current year
findings.detail: The 2026/27 General Fund capital budget was set at £37.579m but has been reduced by £0.197m as a result of overspending in 2025/26, bringing the revised budget to £38.044m after additions (museum redesign and Stone Parish grant).
findings.matters: Prior year capital overspending reduces flexibility in current year; indicates cost control issues carry forward
findings.figures: £0.197m reduction in budget
findings.quote: The budget approved by GAC on 23 February 2026 was £37.579m. The budget for 2026-27 has been reduced by £0.197m as a result of the 2025-26 overspend.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation purchase programme to be unfunded, increasing Capital Financing Requirement by £4.13m
findings.detail: £4.13m of temporary accommodation capital expenditure (property purchases) is expected to be unfunded this year, driving an increase in the council's borrowing requirement (CFR). The council will set aside Minimum Revenue Provision over the life of the properties to fund debt repayment.
findings.matters: Council taking on new capital debt to fund homelessness provision; increases debt service obligations and CFR trajectory
findings.figures: £4.13m unfunded capital spend
findings.quote: £4.13m of expenditure on temporary accommodation units is expected to be unfunded during the year, thereby increasing the Council's Capital Financing Requirement (CFR). The Council will set aside Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) over the life of the houses to fund the purchases.

findings.headline: DTCR Phase 3A Spital Street works expanded after subsurface concrete discovery during construction
findings.detail: Concrete found under the carriageway was not identified in early site investigations. Kent County Council as highways authority required excavation and carriageway reconstruction, increasing scope, working hours, and traffic management complexity. Work expected to complete end July.
findings.matters: Subsurface discovery increases project costs and complexity; demonstrates risk in early site investigation and project delivery
findings.figures: Amount of cost increase not stated
findings.quote: The scope of work has expanded as concrete was found under the carriageway which had not shown up in early site investigations. As highways authority, Kent County Council have required the concrete to be excavated and the carriageway reconstructed.

findings.headline: Dartford Football Club roof insulation found in worse condition than expected, requiring budget revision
findings.detail: During planned sedum roof removal works, moisture mapping revealed insulation in a worsened condition. The council is obtaining estimates for more complex rectification and will report on cost and revised budget by early August. This is described as necessary work requiring capital budget increase.
findings.matters: Capital project discovered to be significantly more expensive than anticipated; budget forecasting accuracy and cost control risk
findings.figures: Budget revision expected; amount not yet quantified
findings.quote: the Council have these results which show a worsened condition than hoped or expected. The property team are obtaining estimates for a more complex rectification and will report on cost and budget in early August. The work will be necessary and a revision to this capital budget is expected to be required.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation property purchases significantly delayed; only partial spend of £347k underspend in 2025/26
findings.detail: The temporary accommodation street purchases programme was £347k below projected spend due to delays in progressing acquisitions. The council noted that identifying suitable properties and completing conveyancing procedures took longer than anticipated, resulting in fewer purchases being completed within the financial period. Full underspend proposed to be rolled forward into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Homelessness prevention and temporary accommodation provision is a growing cost pressure across English councils; delays in acquiring properties suggest the council may struggle to meet housing need and may face increased homelessness pressures or higher interim costs.
findings.figures: Underspend: £347k (rolled forward to 2026/27)
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation street purchases were £347,000 below the projected spend, primarily due to delays in progressing acquisitions. The process of identifying suitable properties and completing the necessary conveyancing procedures took longer than anticipated

findings.headline: Town Centre Transport & Public Realm project incurred contractor compensation events and unforeseen site conditions adding £93k in costs
findings.detail: The Town Centre Transport & Public Realm Improvements overspent by £93k primarily due to contractor compensation events for Phase 3a. These included unforeseen site conditions, additional investigative works, necessary design/construction adjustments (particularly for KCC's full road reconstruction at Spital Street), unexpected reinforced concrete slabs, and high service diversions requiring revised construction methodologies.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted site conditions and required design adjustments indicate either insufficient upfront site investigation or collaboration issues with external partners (KCC), both suggesting execution risk in public realm projects.
findings.figures: Phase 3a overspend: £93k
findings.quote: These events relate to a combination of unforeseen site conditions, additional investigative works, and necessary design or construction adjustments, primarily resulting from works stipulated by Kent County Council for a full reconstruction of the road surfacing at Spital Street

findings.headline: Orchard Theatre design-build project created cost control challenges with £1.098m overspend in 2025/26 due to concurrent design and construction
findings.detail: The Orchard Theatre project, which is being designed and built simultaneously, overspent projection by £1.098m. The report notes that some designs are complex and timescales difficult to predict, with higher-than-expected costs from works commencing earlier than planned. The report describes this as a timing difference rather than true cost increase, with 2026/27 budget reduced to maintain overall project cost.
findings.matters: Design-build projects with concurrent design and construction create inherent cost control risks; this project demonstrates cost forecasting difficulties that required mid-programme budget adjustments.
findings.figures: 2025/26 overspend: £1.098m (described as timing difference, overall project cost to remain unchanged)
findings.quote: This project is unique in that it is being designed and built at the same time. Some of the designs are complex and predicting timescales can be difficult. Higher than expected cost were primarily due to some works being able to commence earlier than planned.

findings.headline: Significant carry-forward budget required for 2026/27 to complete 2025/26 projects, indicating sustained delivery delays
findings.detail: The council is proposing to increase the 2026/27 capital budget by £1.091m to carry forward and complete projects not finished in 2025/26. Major carry-forwards include £367k for window replacement works, £347k for temporary accommodation street purchases (delayed acquisitions), £400k for food waste caddies rollout (delayed to future year), and £1.288k total from housing projects.
findings.matters: Consistent need to carry forward budgets year-on-year suggests either systematic overbudgeting or chronic delivery issues that impair the council's ability to execute capital plans as intended.
findings.figures: Total proposed budget increase: £1.091m. Window replacement carry-forward: £367k, temp accommodation: £347k, food waste caddies: £400k
findings.quote: Cabinet is asked to approve of an overall increase in the 2026/27 capital budget of £1.091m in order to balance the capital programme

findings.headline: External wall rendering programme reduced in scope: only 126 of 154 planned homes completed due to power network complications
findings.detail: The council originally forecasted completing external wall rendering to 154 homes. Due to power network complications, the programme could not proceed in full, and the council completed works to only 126 homes. This represents an 18% reduction in planned scope for this energy performance improvement project.
findings.matters: Scope reduction due to infrastructure constraints beyond the council's control indicates planning risks in large capital programmes and suggests the fuel poverty and energy performance improvement objectives are being delayed.
findings.figures: Planned: 154 homes. Completed: 126 homes. Underspend: £298k
findings.quote: The Council originally forecasted to complete external wall rendering to 154 homes, however due to power network complications, the Council was unable to proceed with the full programme. The Council completed works to 126 homes

findings.headline: Rewiring programme exceeded budget by £140k after failed electrical tests revealed higher-than-forecast defects in council housing stock
findings.detail: The rewiring budget, which consists primarily of works required following failed electrical tests, was originally set at £300k but final outturn was £240k, running £40k above the original budget. The council conducts electrical tests every 5 years on all homes; due to a number of failed tests at the end of the programme, expenditure was higher than the revised forecast of £200k.
findings.matters: The unexpected electrical failures suggest the housing stock has maintenance issues that are more expensive to remediate than anticipated, indicating either deteriorating asset condition or deficient testing/prevention protocols.
findings.figures: Original budget £300k, revised forecast £200k, actual £240k (£40k above original)
findings.quote: The original budget was £300k, with a final forecast made of £200k based on low expenditure at the beginning of the programme. Due to a number of failed tests at the end of the programme, expenditure was higher than forecasted and £40k above the original budget.

findings.headline: Housing maintenance: disabled adaptations £167k under, kitchens/bathrooms £85k under, fascia/soffit £150k under, roof renewals £118k under, window replacement £390k under
findings.detail: Multiple HRA projects experienced underspends due to interim contractor difficulties: disabled adaptations £167k under (mobilisation challenges and reduced productivity), kitchens & bathrooms £85k under (newly appointed interim contractor facing difficulties in mobilising the contract), fascia/soffit replacements £150k under (interim contractor facing difficulties mobilising), and roof renewals £118k under (same contractor issues). Window replacement was £390k under spend primarily because the newly appointed contractor experienced capacity constraints leading to slower-than-expected progress.
findings.matters: Contractor delivery failures indicate the council may struggle to complete its capital programme on time, creating execution risk for any financial agreements predicated on timely asset investment or maintenance.
findings.figures: Disabled adaptations £167k under, kitchens & bathrooms £85k under, fascia/soffit £150k under, roof renewals £118k under, window replacement £390k under
findings.quote: the newly appointed contractor experiencing challenges in managing the workload associated with the contract. These capacity constraints led to slower-than-expected progress, resulting in a lower level of completed works within the period

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - DBC Internal Audit Annual Opinion (July 2026)
findings.headline: Two Critical priority and 12 High priority audit recommendations remain unimplemented and deferred into the next financial year, delaying remediation of known control weaknesses
findings.detail: Of 107 audit actions closed during 2025-26, 27 were carried forward to 2026-27 including 2 Critical and 12 High priority items. The report states that "original risks do remain until implementation is complete," explicitly acknowledging that deferring these actions leaves known control gaps unaddressed. This indicates management is requesting extensions on implementing recommended controls.
findings.matters: Deferred critical and high-priority audit actions demonstrate management is aware of control weaknesses but not remediating them on schedule. This suggests either resource constraints preventing implementation or lower internal priority on governance improvements.
findings.figures: 2 Critical and 12 High priority actions carried forward
findings.quote: When a service is unable to implement actions by the agreed date, they can request a deferral. Deferrals are agreed for valid reasons though the original risks do of course remain until implementation is complete.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - DBC Internal Audit Annual Opinion (July 2026)
findings.headline: Homelessness services audit found incomplete statutory compliance with documented evidence gaps and insufficient case management despite statutory duties under Housing Act 1996
findings.detail: The audit rated homelessness as Limited Assurance, meaning significant gaps in controls. Officers lack documented internal procedures, and audit testing found several cases with incomplete statutory tasks, insufficient notes, and inaccurate or missing information. The audit attributed this to limited resources and capacity constraints, particularly when staff are absent, indicating the council may not have adequate resources to meet its legal obligations.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory duties on homelessness could expose the council to legal action and reputational damage. The resource constraint explanation indicates a structural underfunding rather than a temporary issue.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: However, we found no documented internal processes, procedures, or guidance to support officers in carrying out required actions at each application and duty stage, together with limited resources, capacity constraints, and a lack of resilience during staff absences. As a result, several cases showed incomplete statutory tasks, insufficient notes, and inaccurate or missing information needed to evidence compliance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - DBC Internal Audit Annual Opinion (July 2026)
findings.headline: Families in temporary accommodation rose from 85 to over 320 in five years; council investing in own housing stock to reduce external provider reliance
findings.detail: The audit rated temporary accommodation management as Limited Assurance. The council has responded to the 275% increase in families in temporary accommodation by investing in its own housing stock to reduce reliance on external providers, rather than purchasing services. This represents both a major financial commitment and strategic shift. The audit found the council lacks formal policies and procedures for managing these arrangements.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand capital commitments being driven by demand pressures and whether the council has adequately budgeted and structured governance for this expanding function.
findings.figures: 85 to over 320 families in five years
findings.quote: The number of families in temporary accommodation has risen from around 85 to over 320 in the past five years, creating significant financial pressure. Increased demand has led the Council to invest in its own housing stock to reduce reliance on external providers and increase capacity.

findings.headline: Business rates appeals against £25m of ratable value create a contingent liability of up to £2.3m against current provision
findings.detail: The council identifies business rates appeals as a key budget risk. Total ratable value of £25m is under challenge or appeal, of which the council's 40% share equals £10m. The current provision is £7.7m, creating a potential shortfall of £2.3m if appeals succeed.
findings.matters: This represents a specific, quantified contingent liability that could force unbudgeted expenditure or reserve drawdown if adverse. The provision may be insufficient if appeals succeed partially.
findings.figures: Total ratable value under challenge: £25m; council's share (40%): £10m; current provision: £7.7m
findings.quote: Total ratable value of £25m is under check/ or challenge. 40% is Council's share. Current provision of £7.7m expected to be in place at start of the year

findings.headline: Future capital programme funding is constrained and will rely primarily on drawing down council reserves
findings.detail: The budget statement explicitly notes that 'limited sources have been identified to fund future plans' for capital expenditure. While current capital plans can be funded through capital receipts and reserves, the paper confirms 'Reserves are the main source of the future programme,' indicating the council's capital investment capacity depends on depleting its reserve base.
findings.matters: This signals that the council's future capital investment will require drawing down General Fund and earmarked reserves rather than being funded from revenue or sustainable borrowing. This will erode financial headroom over the medium term.
findings.figures: Capital receipts 'sufficient for current plans but limited sources have been identified to fund future plans'; earmarked reserves total approximately £78m
findings.quote: limited sources have been identified to fund future plans

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs have risen repeatedly over several years, requiring ongoing budget increases
findings.detail: The council explicitly identifies that costs for temporary accommodation for homeless households have continued to increase and necessitated multiple budget increases over several years. This is flagged as a key risk to budget viability, with a specific reserve of £694k allocated but the trend suggests this will remain a structural pressure on the budget.
findings.matters: This demonstrates a demand-driven cost that is growing faster than the council's planned budget envelope, requiring repeated reallocation of resources. For lenders, this signals a spending pressure that is not within the council's direct control and may continue to consume resources.
findings.figures: Homelessness Reserve (694k); costs increased over several years with budgets increased multiple times
findings.quote: These costs have continued to increase and budgets have been increased over several years.

findings.headline: A Revenue Support Grant 'Stepped Reduction' of £2.7m disappears entirely in 2028/29, suggesting a temporary funding cliff or policy assumption that may not hold
findings.detail: The Stepped Reduction in RSG shows (2,732k) in 2027/28 under the baseline, or (1,995k) in the adverse scenario, but then becomes zero in 2028/29. The document does not explain why this reduction is temporary or what causes the recovery. If this assumption fails, the council faces an additional 2m+ funding gap.
findings.matters: Unexplained, temporary reductions in central funding are a red flag; if the recovery does not happen, the council's already fragile financial position collapses further
findings.figures: Stepped Reduction 2027/28: 2,732k (baseline) or 1,995k (adverse); 2028/29: 0
findings.quote: Revenue Support Grant (Stepped Reduction) (2,732) 0 (1,995) 0

findings.headline: Net expenditure gap grows from 9,789k (adverse scenario, 2027/28) to 11,230k (2028/29), an increase of 1,441k
findings.detail: The gap between spending requirements and grant/business rate funding grows by 1,441k in the adverse scenario between 2027/28 and 2028/29. Even with council tax rising to £194.30 per Band D property, this gap cannot be closed without drawing reserves. The council has no identified savings programme large enough to close this gap.
findings.matters: A council unable to balance its budget without reserves, and with the gap widening, faces the prospect of either unsustainable tax rises, service cuts, or insolvency
findings.figures: Net Expenditure (gap): 2027/28: 7,749k (baseline) or 9,789k (adverse); 2028/29: 9,188k (baseline) or 11,230k (adverse)
findings.quote: Net Expenditure 7,749 9,188 9,789 11,230

findings.headline: The council's financial position depends entirely on government grant and business rate assumptions that differ by £1.3m between scenarios
findings.detail: The two scenarios published here differ not in spending plans but in funding expectations. Floor Grant varies from 2,511k to 1,208k in 2027/28 (a 1,303k gap), and from 4,630k to 2,588k in 2028/29 (2,042k gap). This directly drives the reserve drawdown: the adverse scenario's worse funding translates directly into the council drawing down reserves instead of maintaining them.
findings.matters: A council this dependent on central government grant assumptions for financial solvency faces uncontrollable risk; if actual grant settlements match the adverse scenario, reserves deplete rapidly
findings.figures: Floor Grant 2027/28: 2,511k vs 1,208k (1,303k variance); 2028/29: 4,630k vs 2,588k (2,042k variance)

findings.headline: Financial Stability Reserve depletes significantly in the adverse funding scenario, dropping 18% over two years
findings.detail: In the right-hand scenario, the Financial Stability Reserve falls from an opening balance of 30,996k to a closing balance of 25,367k by the end of 2028/29, a drop of 5,629k. The council is using reserves to bridge a widening funding gap: 1,713k drawn in 2027/28 and 2,814k in 2028/29 under this scenario. This trajectory leaves little buffer for future shocks.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion at this rate signals the council is pursuing an unsustainable financial path and will lack flexibility to absorb downturns or unexpected pressures without service cuts or emergency borrowing
findings.figures: FSR opening balance 30,996k, adverse scenario closing balance 2028/29: 25,367k. Use of Reserves: 1,713k (2027/28) and 2,814k (2028/29) in adverse scenario
findings.quote: Financial Stability Reserve Closing Balance 30,996 30,224 29,284 25,367

findings.headline: One-year Adjustment Support Grant of £1.932m masks the structural funding gap until 2027/28.
findings.detail: To protect councils in the first year from the effects of the methodology change, government provided a one-off Adjustment Support Grant. This grant ensures 2026/27 results match the provisional settlement. However, years 2 and 3 will see the negative impact, triggering the reserve draws noted above.
findings.matters: This is a temporary patch that delays rather than solves the underlying funding problem, making the reserve depletion from 2027/28 inevitable.
findings.figures: Adjustment Support Grant £1.932m (2026/27 only)
findings.quote: Given the late change, the government have provided an additional Adjustment Support Grant which means that for the first year of the settlement the results are the same as the provisional settlement.

findings.headline: Final settlement changes business rate pooling methodology, reducing Dartford's funding baseline to the benefit of Kent's upper-tier authority.
findings.detail: The provisional settlement had assumed all business rate pooling gains would go to district councils. The final settlement changed this, now distributing pooling benefits between top-tier and district authorities. In Kent, this means the upper tier benefits at Dartford's expense — a structural reduction in ongoing funding.
findings.matters: This is not a one-off; it applies across the three-year settlement, creating a permanent reduction in the council's funding baseline.
findings.figures: Legacy Business Rates Retention Funding reduced from £13.658m (2025-26 provisional) to £11.509m (2025-26 updated)
findings.quote: The updated methodology in the final settlement has updated the assumption and now shares the benefit of pooling between both top up and tariff authorities, so that in the case of Kent the upper tier authority now has an increased baseline to the detriment of the District Councils.

findings.headline: Council will draw on reserves in 2027/28 and more heavily in 2028/29 to balance the budget; the paper states this approach would not be sustainable in the longer term
findings.detail: The three-year settlement update shows Dartford will need to draw on reserves in 2027/28, with more substantial draws in 2028/29 to maintain a balanced position. Although reserves currently exist to cover this, the paper explicitly states the approach would not be sustainable in the longer term, signalling a structural budget problem.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion indicates a structural budget deficit and declining financial sustainability — a red flag for lenders and a critical issue for the finance director.
findings.figures: 2027/28 and 2028/29 (specific amounts in appendix B(iv) not provided in this extract)
findings.quote: the Council would need to draw on reserves in 2027/28 and more heavily in 2028/29 to maintain a balanced position. Sufficient reserves exist in the short term to achieve this, but the approach would not be sustainable in the longer term.

findings.paper_title: 4.2 Appendix A - Draft Commentary to GAC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Strong investment portfolio of £206.63m underpins capital funding strategy and provides liquidity buffer
findings.detail: The council holds £206.63m in treasury investments as at 31 December 2025, of which £120.90m (58.5%) is in externally managed pooled funds producing investment income budgeted at £5.05m for 2026-27. The council has never suffered an investment loss requiring use of reserves.
findings.matters: The scale and quality of the council's investment portfolio is material to its financial resilience and its ability to fund capital commitments and weather financial stress without resort to market borrowing.
findings.figures: Total investments £206.63m; externally managed pooled funds £120.90m (58.5%); investment income budget £5.05m; unrealised gains on pooled funds >£7m
findings.quote: The Council holds significant invested funds, representing income received in advance of expenditure, plus balances and reserves. In the current financial year to 31 December 2025, the Council's treasury investment balances have ranged between £180.18m and £219.78m.

findings.paper_title: 4.2 Appendix A - Draft Commentary to GAC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Council will fund capital programme through internal borrowing and reserves, not external borrowing, despite £42m lease commitment
findings.detail: Despite the major new capital commitment, the council is not planning external borrowing in 2026/27, choosing instead to fund capital expenditure through capital receipts, reserves, internal borrowing and grants. The liability benchmark is negative, indicating the council is a long-term net investor rather than a long-term net borrower.
findings.matters: Understanding how the council plans to finance its obligations is essential for lenders; the council's strategy to avoid external borrowing despite significant capital needs suggests either strong internal resources or constrained access to markets.
findings.figures: Authorised borrowing limit £60m; external borrowing £23.34m as at 1 February 2026, forecast to fall to £20.44m by March 2027
findings.quote: The Council is not expecting to externally borrow to fund the capital programme during 2026/27 (expenditure is to be funded by capital receipts, reserves, internal borrowing and grants); should there be a requirement to do so, total external borrowing will not exceed the Authorised Limit of £60m.

findings.paper_title: 4.2 Appendix A - Draft Commentary to GAC Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27

findings.matters: A material increase in capital commitments materially affects debt capacity and financial flexibility, and is critical information for lenders assessing creditworthiness.
findings.figures: General Fund CFR rising from £4.62m (31/03/26) to £47.09m (31/03/27); Other debt liabilities £42.57m as at 31/03/27
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase during 2026/27 due to entering into a lease for 139 properties at Knights Reach and due to purchasing new homes for temporary accommodation.

findings.paper_title: DBC04-2425 Estates Compliance Management FINAL Report
findings.headline: Remedial works prioritized by budget availability rather than formal risk assessment, with no documented records
findings.detail: No formalized criteria exists to categorize and risk-assess defects for remedial action. Work approvals happen informally (verbally, by phone, or email) with no formal record-keeping. Email records automatically deleted after 18 months. No monitoring ensures remedial work is actually completed.
findings.matters: Without formal risk assessment, critical safety defects may not be prioritized correctly. Lack of documented records prevents verification of work completion and creates financial control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Email records deleted after 18 months; remedial work handled verbally or by email; no formal prioritization criteria
findings.quote: there is no formalised risk assessment criteria to categorise and prioritise defects identified for remedial action following compliance surveys.

findings.paper_title: DBC04-2425 Estates Compliance Management FINAL Report
findings.headline: Council tracks compliance on spreadsheet with incomplete asset records instead of formal management system
findings.detail: Compliance data tracked on spreadsheet due to limitations in the old Vision system. Survey records stored in Outlook pending migration to new CIPFA system. Asset list incomplete with properties still being identified. No distinction made between council-owned and leasehold properties.
findings.matters: Inadequate systems and incomplete records prevent effective tracking of compliance obligations and increase risk that compliance gaps are missed.
findings.figures: 15 properties examined; survey records in Outlook awaiting CIPFA upload; Vision system being replaced
findings.quote: In the meantime, we were advised that survey reports are currently being stored in Outlook, ready for uploading to CIPFA.

findings.paper_title: DBC04-2425 Estates Compliance Management FINAL Report
findings.headline: Building compliance reporting to senior management has lapsed for three years
findings.detail: Compliance reports showing actual versus target performance were last produced in 2023. No compliance data reports have been requested or produced since. No monitoring mechanisms exist for remedial works or senior management oversight of compliance status.
findings.matters: Without reporting to senior management, the council cannot oversee compliance or ensure corrective actions are taken. This is a fundamental governance and control weakness.
findings.figures: Last compliance report produced in 2023; audit conducted August 2025, report November 2025
findings.quote: compliancy reports (Actual and Targets) was last produced and circulated to management in 2023 and no compliance data reports have been requested or produced since.

findings.paper_title: DBC04-2425 Estates Compliance Management FINAL Report
findings.headline: Statutory building safety compliance checks are months to years overdue on council properties
findings.detail: Of 15 council-occupied properties examined: Gas Safety checks overdue (1 due December 2024, 2 due May 2025); Electrical Installation checks all due in 2023; Asbestos surveys overdue (2 due 2023 and 2024); Fire Risk Assessments not completed on 7 properties marked red. These checks are mandatory under Building Safety Act 2022.
findings.matters: Overdue statutory safety checks create legal and regulatory liability. Building Safety Act 2022 violations could result in enforcement action, injury claims, and service disruption.
findings.figures: Gas Safety: 1 due December 2024, 2 due May 2025. ECIR: 6 overdue (all due 2023). Asbestos: 2 overdue (due 2023-2024). Fire Risk: 7 marked red (no survey on record).
findings.quote: Gas Safety - 3 instances with date for renewed check had been exceeded (1 was due in December 2024 and 2 in May 2025)

findings.paper_title: DBC04-2425 Estates Compliance Management FINAL Report
findings.headline: Internal audit gave 'No Assurance' rating for estates compliance governance
findings.detail: The audit examined governance arrangements for building safety and health & safety compliance across the council's property portfolio and found fundamental gaps and weaknesses requiring immediate action. This is the lowest possible assurance rating.
findings.matters: A No Assurance rating indicates fundamental governance and control failures that would concern any lender assessing council management quality.
findings.figures: 2 critical priority findings with 5 associated actions, 4 high priority findings with 10 actions, total 6 findings with 15 actions
findings.quote: Immediate action is required to address fundamental gaps, weaknesses or non-compliance identified.

findings.headline: Open air theatre identified through compliance checks as requiring full structural reconstruction with immediate action required
findings.detail: Compliance checks have identified the council's open air theatre as requiring full reconstruction with urgent timing requirements. findings.matters: A specific capital project with time-sensitive requirements has been identified, representing material capital commitment and execution complexity that affects the council's financial position and asset liabilities
findings.figures: Cost figures not provided in document
findings.quote: Example – structure checks and remedial work to Open air theatre require a full reconstruction, and timescales for use required immediate action.

findings.headline: Remedial property works currently lack formal risk-assessment criteria, with formal process due end January 2026
findings.detail: The audit identified that remedial works from compliance checks were being decided based on available funds rather than formal risk criteria. The council has committed to producing formal risk-assessment criteria to be finalized by end of January 2026 as part of the Strategic Asset Management Plan, explicitly rejecting the previous approach of prioritizing by funds available.
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance that the council systematically prioritizes identified capital liabilities by risk rather than opportunistically based on cash position, and that governance frameworks are in place to support this
findings.figures: Draft due end of January 2026
findings.quote: Produce a risk-assessment criteria for remedial works (rather than solely basing whether works are done based on funds available). This should be formalised in internal policies and procedures

findings.paper_title: Compliance report to Audit Board Jan 2026
findings.headline: Non-compliance with statutory regulations could result in criminal liability and fines for responsible persons
findings.detail: The council's compliance framework makes clear that failure to meet statutory health and safety obligations carries serious legal consequences. The report explicitly notes that responsible persons could face financial penalties and criminal prosecution, including imprisonment.
findings.matters: Potential criminal and financial liability for non-compliance represents material legal and reputational risk to the council and its senior management
findings.figures: Potential criminal sanctions including prison sentences; unspecified financial penalties
findings.quote: Not meeting them could result in fines or prison sentences for Responsible Persons.

findings.paper_title: Compliance report to Audit Board Jan 2026
findings.headline: Property Services Manager vacancy from December 2024 to August 2025 contributed to compliance management failings
findings.detail: The Property Services Manager position was vacant from December 2024 until August 2025, during which time compliance management failings accumulated. A new appointment was made in August 2025. Senior management acknowledged that the leadership gap contributed to the audit and HSE findings.
findings.matters: Leadership vacancies may indicate management weaknesses and can signal broader organizational challenges in governance and operational capability
findings.figures: Position vacant for 8 months (December 2024 to August 2025)
findings.quote: This was not helped by the lack of a Property Services Manager since December 2024. In August 2025 a new appointment was made to this post.

findings.paper_title: Compliance report to Audit Board Jan 2026
findings.headline: Internal audit rated compliance management as 'No Assurance' with critical and high-priority failings
findings.detail: An internal audit in July 2025 identified 2 critical-ranking issues and 4 high-ranking issues in compliance management across the council's non-housing property portfolio, resulting in a 'No Assurance' audit rating in November 2025. The council has produced an action plan; as of January 2026, four of six compliance areas are completed, one is partially complete, and one remains high-priority pending the Strategic Asset Management Plan.
findings.matters: A 'No Assurance' audit rating indicates significant governance and risk management weaknesses that could affect the council's ability to manage its assets and meet statutory obligations

findings.paper_title: Compliance report to Audit Board Jan 2026
findings.headline: HSE inspection found Dartford non-compliant with asbestos regulations
findings.detail: In November 2025, the Health and Safety Executive inspected the council's asbestos management and concluded it was non-compliant with the Control of Asbestos Regulations. The council has since undertaken corrective action, completing asbestos surveys for directly managed properties and preparing management plans. An HSE re-visit is expected to assess compliance progress.
findings.matters: Regulatory non-compliance creates legal liability and indicates governance weaknesses that could affect the council's operational and financial stability
findings.figures: 100% asbestos surveys completed for directly managed properties; 91 properties requiring asbestos management plans; 17 properties where leaseholder responsibility exists
findings.quote: In November 2025 Property Services were also visited by the HSE as part of their general inspection programme of schools, hospitals and local authorities to assess the suitability of asbestos management. Their findings concluded that Property Services were Non-Compliant with the Control of Asbestos Regulations.

findings.headline: Total debt at £28.24m remains within operational boundary of £90m and authorised limit of £110m as at 30 September 2025
findings.detail: At 30 September 2025, the council's total debt stood at £28.24m (£25.12m borrowing and £3.12m PFI/leases), remaining within the operational boundary of £90m and authorised limit of £110m. The council confirms that all borrowing is within both limits, demonstrating current prudential compliance.
findings.matters: Prudential limit compliance is a fundamental requirement, but the £81.67m CFR forecast in 2026/27 will significantly increase future borrowing needs and consume the current headroom available.
findings.figures: £28.24m actual debt (30.9.2025), £90m operational boundary, £110m authorised limit
findings.quote: All borrowing is within both the operational boundary and authorised limit.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement increases from £34.96m to £81.67m in 2026/27, reflecting lease arrangement
findings.detail: The Capital Financing Requirement (underlying need to borrow for capital purposes) rises 134% from £34.96m at 31 March 2026 to £81.67m at 31 March 2027, with General Fund services CFR increasing from £11.62m to £61.23m. The CFR remains elevated at £78.24m in 2027/28 but will reduce as Minimum Revenue Provision repayments are made each year.
findings.matters: CFR is the key prudential indicator of capital financing need. A 134% increase indicates major new capital commitments that must be financed and serviced, with implications for borrowing levels and debt costs extending across decades.
findings.quote: The CFR increases in 26/27 due to the recognition of the 55-year lease for 138 properties. As the Council makes MRP each year this figure will reduce.

findings.headline: General Fund financing costs forecast at 14.47% of net revenue stream in 2027/28, rising from 7.81% in 2025/26
findings.detail: Interest and repayment costs charged to revenue are forecast to increase from 7.81% of General Fund net revenue stream in 2025/26 to 8.28% in 2026/27, then rise to 14.47% in 2027/28. In cash terms, financing costs grow from £1.68m to £3.19m. The sharp rise in 2027/28 reflects the cost of servicing the lease arrangement once it enters service.
findings.matters: Nearly 15% of net revenue stream consumed by financing costs from 2027/28 significantly constrains resources available for service delivery and is a material indicator of debt sustainability, particularly concerning for councils already under spending pressure.
findings.quote: General fund financing costs (£m) 1.73 1.68 1.90 3.19. Proportion of net revenue stream 6.45% 7.81% 8.28% 14.47%

findings.headline: Council enters 55-year lease for 138 temporary accommodation properties, recognising £38.56m capital expenditure in 2026/27
findings.detail: Dartford has committed to a 55-year lease arrangement for 138 temporary accommodation properties. Under accounting standards, the discounted value of future lease payments must be recognised as capital expenditure. At current PWLB rates, this is estimated at £38.56m and will be recognised in 2026/27 when the properties become available. This single arrangement drives the Capital Financing Requirement from £34.96m to £81.67m in 2026/27.
findings.matters: A 55-year commitment for temporary accommodation signals sustained housing pressure and creates a multi-decade payment obligation. The large upfront capital recognition substantially increases borrowing requirement and finance costs, constraining the council's financial flexibility for decades.
findings.figures: £38.56m capital recognition, 138 properties, 55-year term, CFR increase to £81.67m
findings.quote: The Council has entered into a 55-year lease arrangement for 138 properties for temporary accommodation. The Council has to recognise the discounted value of the future lease payments under this arrangement as capital expenditure. The value to be recognised will depend on the relevant PWLB borrowing rate at the point the properties become available (scheduled in 2026/27). At current rates the value to be recognised is estimated at £38.56m.

news_drafts.headline: Dartford: Orchard Theatre forecasts overspend, with extra funding request due at November Cabinet
news_drafts.lead:
Dartford Council's Cabinet papers for 29 October show the Orchard Theatre project is forecasting an overspend against its approved budget. A request for additional funding will go to Cabinet in November. The paper gives no figure. It says the theatre remains on track to reopen as scheduled, with partial practical completion on 6 December and some elements still to finish.

The temporary Orchard West theatre is forecast to overspend its £360,000 budget, which is paid for from money set aside (reserves), by £95,000. Projected spend is £455,000, and £453,730 had been incurred by the end of September. Air conditioning costs of £100,000 are excluded from the estimate. The paper says the overspend will be considered at the full projection exercise, with a view to offsetting it against underspends elsewhere this year.

In council housing, the housing revenue account (the separate, ring-fenced account for the council's own homes, paid for by rents) has a projected deficit of £497,610 for 2026/27 in the mid-year projection, against £659,090 in the current budget. Repairs and maintenance is projected to be overspent by £500,000, including extra delivery costs for the outgoing contractor, TSG Building Services PLC. The paper says the overspend has no significant impact on the account's ongoing viability. Roof renewals are forecast to overspend by about £0.300m, which the council says is needed to keep its housing stock compliant. An anticipated underspend on window replacement is expected to offset it.
